sourceNote: Reviewed all supplied events E0–E3321. Attribution uses the supplied text and conversational continuity; no audio was available. Numerous events contain both a previous speaker's final words and the next speaker's reply; these are U. Transcription errors and unmarked brief interjections limit precision. Candidates concern proposed protective arguments, not confirmed unsupported slogans. Quoted third-party positions and expressly limited hypotheticals are not treated as the speakers' unconditional commitments.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: only an omniscient or near omniscient mind could make the Judgment call
candidates.explanation: Historical interdependence supplies an ordinary reason for uncertainty, rather than replacing one. Requiring near omniscience could nevertheless block any suffering-based objection without assessing its particulars (E1887–1910). Whether that protection is adopted remains unclear: B raises ethical qualifications and subsequently says he would abandon skeptical theism before ordinary moral judgment (E1983–2011).

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: when evidence is inscrutable on some hypothesis even if it's high given another one the evidence can't adjudicate between them
candidates.explanation: The proposed rule explicitly removes religious confusion's discriminatory force despite its admitted likelihood under naturalism (E2185–2228). Complexity and free-choice constraints supply reasons, so this is a protected non-slogan argument; the unresolved bridge is from unknown likelihood to evidential neutrality. B explicitly doubts whether this proposed defense works and identifies its additional assumption (E2215–2228).

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: we don't know nearly enough to make the claim that there is a better set of circumstances
candidates.explanation: After A's reply, B renews the complexity defense: inaccessible consequences and free-choice facts allegedly prevent identifying any better world (E2314–2334). This could immunize observed evils, but the passage also presents a contestable argument on defenders' behalf, says it may be wrong, and requests substantive criticism (E2334–2339). Blanket protective use therefore remains uncertain.

contrasts.speaker: A
contrasts.quote: I'm not saying this General observation trumps that
contrasts.explanation: A expressly limits his criticism of inconsistent appeals to cognitive limitations. After providing cosmological and fine-tuning examples, he allows that their merits may differ and requires examining the particulars; his earlier characterization as excuses does not replace that examination.

contrasts.speaker: B
contrasts.quote: there is some impact that peer disagreement ought to have on one's confidence in theism
contrasts.explanation: B accepts A's correction and explains why complexity and expert disagreement should reduce confidence. He distinguishes that concession from accepting a particular probability or atheism, making the conclusion explicitly limited and responsive to the preceding reasons.
